subsection: 3. Primary and secondary social groups, kinship, socialisation

notes.b: A social group is two or more people who interact regularly and share a sense of belonging, such as a purpose, an identity or a place. Groups differ in how close and how formal their relationships are, and a crowd of strangers is not a group.
points: A primary group is small, intimate and face-to-face, with long-lasting relationships; examples are the family and close friends.
Primary groups meet emotional needs and give a sense of belonging, so they shape a person's personality, values and sense of identity. They are also where primary socialisation mainly happens.

A secondary group is larger and more formal, with relationships that are impersonal and often short-term or limited to a role; examples are a school class, a workplace, a trade union, a sports club and a political party.
Secondary groups are organised around a specific goal, such as completing a course or producing goods. Members often join by choice and leave when the purpose is finished.

To compare them: primary groups are small, close, lasting and personal, while secondary groups are larger, formal, often temporary and purpose-based. A person belongs to both types at once, and some groups, such as a small close-knit club, sit between the two.
An in-group is a group with which a person identifies and feels loyalty; an out-group is a group that members see as different from or opposed to their own.
A reference group is a group whose norms and values (the standards of behaviour it expects) a person uses to judge their own behaviour, even if they are not a member of it.
A peer group is made up of people of similar age and status. It is important in adolescence and can act as a primary or a secondary agent of socialisation, depending on how close its members are.
notes.tip: Primary and secondary groups are separated by the type of relationship (close, personal and lasting versus formal, impersonal and purpose-based), not by size alone or the order in which you join them. Don't say primary groups are always more important; say they shape personality early and strongly.

notes.b: Kinship is the network of family ties between people who are related by blood, marriage or adoption. It is a relationship, not a type of household, so it includes relatives who live apart.
points: Kinship means family ties: relationships based on blood (common ancestry or lineage), marriage or adoption.
Consanguineal kin are related by blood, for example parents, children, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins.

Affinal kin are related through marriage, for example a spouse, a spouse's parents, who are in-laws, and step-relatives. The terms consanguineal and affinal are optional; blood and marriage are enough.
A nuclear family is parents and their dependent children living together as one household.
An extended family includes kin beyond the nuclear family, such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, who live together or keep in close contact.
The family of orientation is the family a person is born into; the family of procreation is the family a person forms through their own marriage or partnership and children.
Kinship is found in every society, which is part of why the family is called universal.
Descent, the line through which kinship is traced, can run through the mother's side, the father's side or both; most modern Western societies trace both sides.
notes.tip: Don't define kinship as 'the extended family'. An extended family is a household or network pattern, while kinship is the relationship itself. In explain-the-term questions, give family ties by blood, marriage or common ancestry, plus an example.

notes.h: What kin do for each other
notes.b: Kin networks matter because relatives are often the first people to turn to when help is needed. They have also changed as society has changed.
points: Kin networks provide practical and emotional support, including childcare, financial help, care for older members and a sense of identity.
Kinship obligations include mutual support and, in many societies, inheritance rights between relatives.
Kin networks have become looser as families have become smaller and more mobile, but relatives keep in contact through phones and social media.

notes.b: Socialisation is the lifelong process by which people learn the norms, values, behaviour, roles and skills of their society and so become members of it. Without it a child could not use language or form relationships.
points: Socialisation is lifelong, so it continues in adolescence and adulthood as well as in childhood.
Primary socialisation takes place in early childhood, mainly within the family, where children learn language, toilet training, manners, self-control, right from wrong and a first sense of identity.

Secondary socialisation takes place later in wider settings such as school, the peer group, the workplace, religious institutions and the media. There people learn the roles and norms of that setting, such as punctuality, rules, teamwork and respect for authority.

Through socialisation the culture of a society is passed from one generation to the next, which maintains continuity over time. It also produces conformity and social order and lets individuals take part in society.

People learn through observation, imitation, rewards and punishments (sanctions), role models and direct instruction. In the family, children learn through observation, imitation and consistent discipline.
Anticipatory socialisation is learning the norms of a role or group that a person hopes to join, such as a student learning workplace norms before starting an apprenticeship.
Resocialisation is learning new norms after a major change in life, such as entering the army or prison, where old habits are replaced.
notes.tip: Say that socialisation is lifelong, mainly through the family and then school, work and media; writing only 'learning in childhood' loses a mark. Don't confuse primary socialisation (early childhood, mainly in the family) with a primary group.

notes.b: Agents of socialisation are the people and institutions that pass on norms and values. Each one teaches something different.
points: The main agents are the family, school, peer group, mass media, religion and the workplace.
School socialises formally through the curriculum and informally through the hidden curriculum, the unwritten lessons taught by its rules and routines.
The peer group becomes an important agent in adolescence, when young people test independence and learn the norms of their age group.
Mass media, including television, the internet and social media, transmit norms and values and shape consumer habits.
notes.tip: Education is only one agent of socialisation, so don't treat the two as the same. For school, mention reinforcing behaviour learned at home, punctuality, respect for authority, rules, sharing, teamwork and the hidden curriculum.

notes.b: Monogamy is one form of marriage; the other forms are classed as polygamy. It describes how many partners a person has at one time.
points: Monogamy is marriage, or a partnership, with one partner at a time, traditionally one husband and one wife.
Monogamy is the norm in the Western world, and it is the only form of marriage recognised in Ireland. It is not the only form worldwide.
Polygamy is marriage to more than one spouse at the same time; polygyny is one man with several wives, and polyandry is one woman with several husbands. Both are found in some other societies.
Polygamy is illegal in Ireland.
Bigamy is entering a marriage while still legally married to another person, without the death or divorce of the first spouse. It is an offence in Ireland.
Serial monogamy is a succession of monogamous marriages, one after another, following divorce or the death of a spouse.
Spouses in a monogamous marriage are expected to remain faithful and loyal to each other, live together, and support one another and their children financially.
Civil and religious marriages are both legally recognised in Ireland, and both are monogamous. Same-sex marriage is also lawful in Ireland and is monogamous, being a marriage of two people.
notes.tip: Define monogamy as one partner at a time and give an example from Irish life, such as a husband and wife. Don't call it the only form of marriage worldwide; it is the norm in Western societies and the only one lawful in Ireland. In a set of terms, answer each separately.

keyTerms.definition: A small, intimate, face-to-face group with long-lasting relationships, such as the family.
A larger, formal group organised around a specific goal, with impersonal relationships, such as a school or workplace.
A group with which a person identifies and feels loyalty.
A group whose norms and values a person uses to judge their own behaviour.
The network of relationships between people related by blood, marriage or adoption.
The lifelong process by which people learn the norms, values, roles and skills of their society.
Learning the norms of a role or group that a person hopes to join.
Learning new norms after a major change in life.
Marriage between one husband and one wife at a time.
Marriage to more than one spouse at the same time.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a primary social group and a secondary social group, giving one example of each.
questions.model: A primary group is small, intimate and face-to-face, with long-lasting relationships, for example the family or close friends. It meets emotional needs and shapes personality. A secondary group is larger and more formal, with impersonal and often short-term relationships, organised around a goal, for example a school, a workplace or a trade union.

questions.prompt: Explain how the family and other agents of socialisation prepare a child for adult life, and discuss the part played by kinship in supporting family members.
questions.model: Socialisation is the lifelong process by which people learn the norms, values, roles and skills of their society. Primary socialisation takes place in early childhood, mainly in the family, where children learn language, self-control and basic norms. Secondary socialisation takes place in school, through the peer group, in religious institutions, in the workplace and through the media. The peer group becomes important in adolescence, when young people test independence and learn the norms of their age group. Anticipatory socialisation prepares a person for a role they hope to take up, and resocialisation replaces old norms after a major change. Through socialisation culture passes from one generation to the next. Kinship is the network of relationships based on blood, marriage or adoption. Consanguineal kin are related by blood and affinal kin through marriage. Extended family members provide childcare, financial help and care for older relatives, and kin networks give practical and emotional support in times of difficulty. Kinship obligations include mutual support and inheritance in many societies.
